title: Adaptive proxy pacing & connection windowing — latency sweep (Aug 2026)
content:
Summary:
This is the working notes for a set of microbenchmarks focused on how proxy-side pacing and TCP/HTTP windowing interact with streaming LLM inference. Goal: identify low-effort mitigations we can ship in the proxy (Envoy-based edge) that reduce tail latency (P99) during high-concurrency, bursty traffic without sacrificing median throughput.

Motivation / hypothesis:
- Observed customer incidents where short microbursts cause P99 spikes even when average QPS is well within capacity (see RWINF-1234).
- Hypothesis: small TCP/HTTP/HTTP2 flow-control windows and naive per-request flush behavior from client SDKs amplify head-of-line blocking and create network-side stalls that the runtime/kvcache sees as long gaps (cold KV cache windows) and therefore amplify on-device compute tails.
- Secondary hypothesis: adding an adaptive pacing layer in the proxy to smooth send-side chunking can reduce serialization bursts across competing streams and reduce P99 without significant increases in median latency.

Testbed:
- Cluster: dedicated inference pool in us-west1 (8x A100/80GB nodes).
- Edge: Envoy 1.27 deployed as external edge proxy + upstream route to ASG of inference workers.
- Model: small reproducible generation model (instruction-tuned 13B equivalent, eval config: 64 tokens requested, prompt ~64 tokens, max_context 512).
- Runtime config: batch size fixed at 8, kv cache enabled, continuous batching on.
- Load generators:
  - HTTP:wrk2 (HTTP/1.1 chunked + HTTP/2 via h2c where supported)
  - gRPC: ghz (for unary and streaming flavors)
- Client-side knobs: chunk-size (bytes), flush-frequency (ms), pipeline/concurrency per connection.
- Measured signals: per-request total latency, time-to-first-byte (TTFB), stream inter-chunk gaps, p50/p90/p95/p99, tokens/sec, CPU/GPU utilization, Envoy upstream/downstream buffer usage.

Experiment matrix (high-level):
- Variable A: protocol (HTTP/1.1 chunked, HTTP/2, gRPC streaming)
- Variable B: proxy send-window / connection settings (default, reduced to 64KB, increased to 512KB)
- Variable C: client chunking behavior (no-chunk flush-on-end, 512B chunks every 10ms, 4KB chunks every 2ms)
- Variable D: adaptive pacing enabled in proxy (off, naive fixed-rate, adaptive based on downstream queue length)
- Traffic patterns: steady QPS (200 QPS), bursty (sawtooth 50–400 QPS every 10s), microburst (instant jump 0->400 QPS).

Representative commands (notes, not exact automation yet):
- wrk2 -t8 -c200 -d120s -R200 --header "Connection: keep-alive" http://edge/proxy/gen
- ghz --insecure -proto api.proto -call Gen.Stream -concurrency 50 -n 20000 --data request.json edge:443

Key observations (raw):
1) HTTP/1.1 chunked with small client-side chunks (512B / 10ms) produced lower median but higher P99 vs 4KB chunks. Numbers (example run, bursty workload): p50=110ms, p95=220ms, p99=630ms (512B chunks); p50=125ms, p95=240ms, p99=410ms (4KB chunks).
2) HTTP/2 streaming with default flow-control saw less P99 amplification vs HTTP/1.1 when connection concurrency is high, but only when many independent streams share the same connection. When clients open many short-lived connections, HTTP/2 benefit vanishes.
3) gRPC streaming (client-streaming style for tokens) reduces round-trips but is sensitive to upstream window sizes; with default Envoy upstream window we observed occasional 100–200ms stalls in inter-chunk spacing leading to spiky P99.
4) Reducing TCP send buffer sizes at proxy (to ~64KB) increased contention and pushed serialization: P99 worsened by ~30% in most burst patterns. Increasing to 512KB improved P99 slightly (~10%) but increased median by ~5–10ms.
5) Enabling a naive fixed-rate pacing layer in Envoy (emit at X KB/s per-stream) reduced P99 by ~25% in the microburst scenario, but hurt throughput when load was sustained at peak.
6) Adaptive pacing (emit tokens with a feedback loop based on upstream queue length and observed inter-chunk gaps) reduced P99 by ~40% for microbursts with <5% impact on median and maintained tokens/sec at steady-state.

Detailed micro-interpretation:
- Root cause appears to be a combination of three effects:
  1) Client SDKs that aggressively flush tiny chunks cause bursts of small packets which the proxy serializes (per-connection) and then the runtime sees as uneven arrival of KV cache deltas.
  2) TCP/HTTP flow-control and small send/recv buffers induce head-of-line blocking across streams on a single connection, especially for HTTP/1.1 and gRPC over HTTP/2 with conservative windows.
  3) Proxy CPU scheduling and packetization (Envoy worker thread that serializes writes) shows microqueues where multiple small writes are batched together and then flushed with gaps — these gaps align badly with the model's compute pipeline and cause cold-kv windows and tail latency amplification.

Recommendations (short-term, low-effort):
- Implement an opt-in adaptive pacing filter in the proxy:
  - heuristic: measure per-upstream-queue length (bytes) + measured inter-chunk gap for last N chunks. If upstream queue > threshold or gap variance > threshold, smooth outbound writes by capping instantaneous chunk emission and queuing small writes for up to T ms (T configurable, default 5ms).
  - feature flag behind runtime-config.
- Increase default HTTP/2 initial stream window on the Envoy-to-upstream path for dedicated inference clusters (512KB default) — add experiment flag to rollback if worst-case memory usage is unacceptable.
- Update client SDK docs: recommend batching small token flushes into >=2KB chunks or adding 2–5ms micro-delays when streaming from constrained clients (mobile, low-power).
- Add observability: per-request inter-chunk-gap histogram, proxy-side per-connection write queue depth gauge, and an alert when P99 / gap-rate correlation exceeds threshold.

Longer-term experiments / follow-ups:
- Evaluate combining adaptive pacing with request coalescing at the proxy (group tiny concurrent writes destined for the same upstream to reduce write syscalls). Risk: increased end-to-end latency for very small requests — need SLO-based guardrails.
- Measure against real customer traffic (non-synthetic) via a canary with 1% traffic and observability hooks.
- Explore kernel/TCP tweaks on workers: tcp_small_queues vs tcp_mtu_probing; but prefer app-level mitigations first.

Open questions / unknowns:
- How do these heuristics interact with TLS record sizes? (Envoy currently splits writes at TLS boundaries; we need to see if pacing still effective under TLS records).
- Impact on egress costs (extra bytes due to coalescing vs pacing) is small but should be calculated for billing-sensitive customers.
- Edge-cases: clients behind aggressive NATs / carrier-grade NATs that drop long-lived connections — our recommendation to use HTTP/2 assumes connection longevity which may not hold everywhere.

Quick action plan (next 2 weeks):
- Week 0: prototype adaptive pacing filter in a branch of proxy repo (PR link above). Implement config knobs and local unit tests. (owner: Jordan Li)
- Week 1: run full experiment matrix on staging with 3 repeats per cell, collect p50/p95/p99 and per-chunk-gap traces (owner: Samir Patel).
- Week 2: deploy as 1% canary to production edge fleet in us-west1, monitor for regressions. If P99 improves and no regressions, roll to 10% and then global (owner: Evelyn Cho + SRE).

Notes / scratchpad:
- Raw sample CDF for one microburst run (HTTP/1.1, no pacing): 90% <= 230ms, 95% <= 360ms, 99% <= 630ms, 99.9% <= 1.2s.
- With adaptive pacing (same run): 90% <= 205ms, 95% <= 260ms, 99% <= 380ms, 99.9% <= 620ms.
- Tickets created: RWINF-1234 (incident), RWINF-1301 (adaptive-pacing-proxy-filter).

Edits / TODOs:
- Clean up automation scripts and add exact wrk2/ghz commands used for each cell.
- Add CSV of raw numbers + small ASCII sparkline in a follow-up.
- Validate memory cost of larger HTTP/2 windows across 1000s of concurrent streams — get SRE input.

End of notes.
